extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical poetics and literature
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated commentary on Aristotle's Art of Poetry setting out theoretical criteria for what poetry is, how different poetic arts imitate, their means, parts, subjects, manners, and the effects they should produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as Imitation (Mimesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever employs means to shew and represent any subject, as naturally as may be, whether it does really exist or no, is called Imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a thing to be called Imitation it is necessary that four things be seen at the same time: that which imitates; that which is imitated; the instrument or means which is made use of; and the manner in which they are employed. Example: Homer putting himself in the person of a character is 'exact imitation'; mere narration is a less direct imitation. Anti-pattern: treating verse-form alone as the defining feature of poetry instead of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Four Constituent Elements of Imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: That which imitates; that which is imitated; the instrument or means which is made use of; and the manner in which they are employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation or creation of poetic works should check all four: source (the imitator), object (what's imitated), medium (voice, music, verse, acting), and manner (narration vs enacted performance). Missing any of these undermines true mimesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of Imitation: Number, Discourse, and Harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: Dithyrambicks, Nomes, Tragedy and Comedy employ equally those three Means: Number, Discourse and Harmony; that is to say, Music (with differences in use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number (rhythm/measure), Discourse (prose or verse), and Harmony (music/song) are the technical means to judge how an imitation is effected. Some arts use them together (drama), others separately (dance uses number; some music uses harmony and number without words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number (Rhythm) as Order of Movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Number or Rhythm signifies properly a measured cadence, or a regulated movement; the Order of Movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess rhythm and cadences as integral to poetic effect. Distinguish Number in verse from Number present in instrumental tunes without words (which Plato criticises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse as Prose or Verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourse is a general term and comprehends either Prose or Verse; epopaeia (epic) may include plain discourses which are prose deprived of number and harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating genre and technique, judge how discourse (narration, dialogue, verse) functions; epic can be in prose or verse and should be categorized by imitation not by meter alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony (Music/Song) as Order of Sounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony signifies only Music or Song here; the order of sounds which arises from the mixture of sharp and grave tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In works that include music/chorus, evaluate the contribution of melodic order; beware of purely instrumental tunes without words that may leave the understanding without action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts: Quantity and Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain the number and quality of all its parts — as well the parts of Quantity as Quality — for every sort of Poeſie is composed of a certain number of parts which are different and distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze both quantitative structure (e.g., divisions, length, meter) and qualitative components (themes, modes of imitation, instruments) when judging a poem's completeness and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject Constitution for a Good Poem
rubrics_metrics.description: To shew in what manner a Subject must be constituted to make a good Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem's subject should be arranged to achieve the intended imitation and effect (e.g., heroic actions for epic, noble actions for tragedy). Selecting appropriate subjects is the principal and most difficult task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's Intended Effects on Minds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Effects which they ought to produce in Minds. For Example, Tragedy ought to refine the passions, by the Means of Terror and Pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem attains its ethical/aesthetic ends: tragedy should evoke and refine emotions (terror, pity); other genres have their own intended moral/psychological impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and Established Rules (Art vs Chance vs Custom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method has often been used for Art; he that speaks of Method, speaks of established Rules and a way marked out whereby we may certainly arrive at what we seek for, and this is what we call Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that combine art (rule/skill) and custom/natural genius. Anti-patterns: works produced only by chance or by custom without rule may be inexact or insipid; strictly rule-bound but unnatural works can be flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin from Nature / Foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall imitate Nature, and begin with the first strokes. For Nature always begins with that which is the foundation of the rest, and postpones Effects to their Causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose and evaluate by starting from foundational causes and simple elements before moving to complex effects; ensure the work's structure reflects natural causal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genres Classified by Imitation, Not Meter
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be more just to call the first a Poet, and the second a Philosopher… the Invention and Imitation, and not the Verse which makes the Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not classify poets or works solely by verse-type (hexameter, elegiac, iambic). Instead classify by the kind of imitation (epic, tragedy, comedy) and the subject/manner of imitation. Anti-pattern: labeling Empedocles and Homer the same 'epic' just because of meter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic (Epopœia) Broad Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Epopœia is a genus encompassing all sorts of poems whether in Prose or Verse; all of them are the same Imitations, so give them one name by which you may know their Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating epics, consider narrative/epic qualities rather than fixed meter; epopœia may embrace prose romances and farces insofar as they are imitative discourses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dance and Music as Distinct Imitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Dancers make use of Number only. When Music and Dancing are found together, they are two different Arts, two different Imitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat dance (movement/rhythm) separately from music/verse in evaluation and composition. When combined (e.g., chorus) assess each art's imitation contribution independently and their interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of Imitation (How it is Done)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third difference consists in the manner in which these Imitations are made… either in making a Narration, or acting some other Person… or by always making those act which we imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish narrative (Homeric) from enacted/dramatic imitation (Sophocles) and from other modes (shifting person vs staying as narrator). This affects tone, immediacy, and audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of Human Character (Better/Worse/As They Are)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions must be either good, or bad… Poets in their Imitations must represent Men in respect to us, either better or worse, or just as we are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ethical/representational stance: tragedy tends to represent men better (noble swelling of character), comedy older forms represented them worse, and some works aim for likeness. Consider moral effects and whether depiction provokes emulation or correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Classifying by Verse Mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one should think it advisable to make a Poem of all the different sorts of Verse... he is not to be called Heroick, Elegiac, or Iambic merely by his metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that mixing meters does not alter the essential genus of the poem; classification should rely upon imitation and subject rather than surface metrical combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunes Without Words Leave Understanding Without Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato condemns these Tunes without Words, for they leave the Understanding without Action, and it is to that the Poets ought to speak, to instruct, and reform it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When music or instrumental passages appear without words, consider whether they contribute to intellectual/moral action; if not, they may be judged deficient in poetic purpose.
